```{r prediction-comparison-plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
p_ols <- ggplot(preds_df, aes(x = OLS, y = Actual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = skittles[1]) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "maroon") +
  labs(title = "OLS (COPD)", x = "Predicted", y = "Actual") +
  theme_minimal()

p_en <- ggplot(preds_df, aes(x = Elastic_Net, y = Actual)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = skittles[3]) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "maroon") +
  labs(title = "Elastic Net (COPD)", x = "Predicted", y = "Actual") +
  theme_minimal()

p_ols + p_en
```

**Figure 19. Predictions Plot for Elastic Net vs. OLS Regression (COPD)**

---

# 7. Conclusions & Comparison to Pneumonia

**Question 32** [4 points]: What conclusions do you make? Compare COPD vs. pneumonia. What recommendations for the client?
> ##
 **Data and pipeline differences from pneumonia**: The COPD merged dataset contained 71 columns after feature selection compared to 81 for pneumonia, reflecting the absence of the COPD specific payment measure and hospital return days variable that CMS does not publish for COPD in the FY2024 data. Three ComparedToNational columns were dropped due to near zero variance, a larger number than pneumonia, indicating that for COPD specific outcome measures, almost all hospitals fall into the same national comparison category, leaving little discriminating information. Two variables were dropped after missForest imputation due to extremely high OOB error (Intensive Care Unit Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis and Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis), consistent with their extreme missingness of 3,234 and 2,431 NAs respectively.
>
> **Target variable**: Our COPD predicted readmission rate (mean ~19.0%, range ~11.7–28.2%) is notably higher than pneumonia (~16.5%, range ~10.9–25.3%), confirming the clinical literature that COPD carries one of the highest 30 day readmission burdens of any CMS tracked condition. The correlation matrix showed PredictedReadmissionRate correlates strongly with ExpectedReadmissionRate (r = 0.83) and moderately with observed rate (r = 0.76), validating our target choice.
>
> **Model performance — the central finding**: The COPD OLS and Elastic Net models both achieved a test R² of approximately 0.18 and adjusted R² of 0.143. This is less than half the explanatory power of the pneumonia model (~0.39). This is not a modeling failure. It is the most important substantive finding of this analysis. COPD is a chronic condition where patient level disease severity (FEV₁, GOLD staging, exacerbation history, smoking status, comorbidity burden) drives the majority of readmission risk, and none of this is captured in any hospital level CMS dataset. The hospital level features we have access to explain only about 14 to 18% of why some hospitals have higher COPD readmission rates than others. The remaining 82 to 86% is driven by factors outside our data.
>
> **Key predictor differences from pneumonia**: The Elastic Net importance plot revealed that Emergency department volume was by far the dominant predictor for COPD (importance = 100), followed by State (~65), Median ED time (~52), and Staff responsiveness (~51). This contrasts sharply with pneumonia where hospital return days, infection control proxies (MRSA, vaccination), and Medicare spending ranked highest. For COPD, infection control variables (MRSA Bacteremia, influenza vaccination) ranked near the bottom of the importance list. This shift from infection control dominance in pneumonia to operational and geographic dominance in COPD is clinically coherent: pneumonia is an acute communicable disease where hospital infection control directly affects outcomes, while COPD is a chronic non communicable condition where operational factors like ED strain and geographic disease burden matter more.
>
> **Clustering**: The k means analysis identified 2 clusters of hospitals, separated primarily along the patient communication and satisfaction dimension rather than clinical severity. Cluster 2 (higher performing) showed notably better discharge information scores (~87 vs ~82), communication about medicines (~75 vs ~71), and lower predicted readmission rates (~18% vs ~20%). Death rate for COPD patients and perioperative embolism rate were nearly identical across clusters, confirming that clinical complexity does not drive the segmentation. Communication and discharge quality does. This is directly actionable for the watchdog.
>
> **Recommendations to the client**: 
>1. First, for patients choosing a hospital for COPD related care, the watchdog should highlight Emergency department volume and median ED wait time as the most predictive publicly available hospital level metrics more so than the satisfaction measures that dominate the pneumonia recommendation. Hospitals with lower ED volume and shorter wait times showed consistently lower predicted COPD readmissions in our model. 
>2. Second, discharge information and communication about medicines scores remain important secondary metrics. Hospitals in Cluster 2 with higher scores on these measures achieved meaningfully lower readmission rates, and these are metrics patients can look up before choosing a hospital. 
>3. Third, and most importantly, we recommend the watchdog advocate for CMS to integrate patient level COPD severity data (GOLD staging, FEV₁, prior exacerbation history) with hospital level reporting before using COPD readmission rates as standalone public quality metrics. An adjusted R² of only 0.143 means these hospital level rates are dominated by patient mix factors that CMS has not fully controlled for, and penalizing hospitals under the HRRP based on metrics with this little hospital attributable variance risks unfairly punishing hospitals that serve the most severely ill COPD patients. 
>4. Fourth, a composite respiratory readmission indicator combining COPD and pneumonia should be explored. Hospitals performing poorly on both conditions likely have systemic respiratory care deficiencies that are more reliably attributable to hospital quality than either condition alone. Finally, non linear models such as random forest should be explored in follow up analyses to determine whether any non linear relationships between these predictors and COPD readmissions could improve model fit beyond the ceiling imposed by our current linear approach.
